B
At a rightward fork the upper parental template runs 3′ to 5′ from left to right. Which newly synthesized region grows rightward?
Upper-template daughter|Lower-template daughter|Both individual lagging fragments|Neither
A

The upper template is read 3′ to 5′ toward the fork. The lower-template daughter grows leftward in individual fragments. The direction of fork advance is not the direction of every polymerization event.
B
Which Pol III core subunit provides the major proofreading activity?
α|ε|θ|β
B
Epsilon (dnaQ) removes nucleotides from the 3′ terminus. Alpha polymerizes, theta associates with epsilon, and beta is a separate sliding clamp.
B
Which activity distinguishes intact E. coli Pol I from ordinary Klenow fragment?
5′ nuclease|5′ to 3′ polymerization|3′ to 5′ proofreading|DNA binding
A
The N-terminal 5′ nuclease domain is missing from Klenow; the large fragment retains polymerization and normally proofreading.
B
What is the immediate leaving group during dCTP incorporation into DNA?
CMP|ATP|Pyrophosphate|NAD+
C
The alpha phosphate remains in the new backbone and beta plus gamma depart as pyrophosphate. NAD+ is a ligase cofactor, not a polymerase substrate.
B
DnaB translocates along which strand in a normal E. coli elongating fork?
Leading daughter 3′ to 5′|Lagging template 5′ to 3′|Leading template 5′ to 3′|Lagging daughter 3′ to 5′
B
DnaB surrounds the parental lagging template and moves 5′ to 3′. Neither daughter strand is its normal tracking substrate.
B
What does a beta clamp directly contribute to Pol III?
De novo RNA synthesis|Proofreading chemistry|Retention on DNA|NAD-dependent sealing
C
The ring promotes processivity by keeping polymerase associated with DNA. Primase, epsilon and LigA perform the other activities.
B
Which enzyme uses NAD+ in its normal E. coli replicative role?
LigA|DnaB|DnaG|GyrB
A
LigA uses NAD+ to form an enzyme–AMP intermediate. DnaB and gyrase use nucleotide hydrolysis for movement or conformational cycling; DnaG uses ribonucleotides for RNA synthesis.
B
A DNA-only nick has a 3′ hydroxyl and adjacent 5′ phosphate. What is required to restore the missing bond?
Primase|Ligase|Helicase|A DNA polymerase adding a base
B
No base is missing. Ligase activates the 5′ phosphate and joins the adjacent ends; polymerase is needed for gaps rather than an already correctly aligned nick.
B
Which is the major duplex decatenase in E. coli?
DnaG|Topoisomerase I|Topoisomerase IV|Pol II
C
Topo IV uses type II strand passage to remove daughter-duplex interlinks. Topo I is primarily a negative-supercoil relaxase.
B
Tus–Ter is best described as:
An obligatory universal bacterial termination enzyme|A polar protein-DNA barrier in E. coli|A ligase that seals the last nick|A eukaryotic telomerase complex
B
Tus binds asymmetric Ter sites and can arrest forks from one direction. It does not synthesize DNA or execute all completion steps.
B
Which statement best describes Pol II in E. coli?
Main bulk replicase|Major primer-removal nuclease|A polymerase involved in damage-associated synthesis and recovery|An ATP-dependent helicase
C
Pol II has polymerase and proofreading activities and participates in repair/recovery contexts. Pol III carries out bulk chromosome copying and Pol I processes primers.
B
Why is primase needed even when all four dNTPs are plentiful?
Polymerase lacks a normal de novo initiation ability|Polymerase reads RNA only|DNA cannot pair with DNA|Primase makes all deoxyribonucleotides
A
A template and dNTPs are insufficient without an existing primer 3′ hydroxyl. DnaG provides this using a short RNA chain.
B
Which distinction between rate and processivity is correct?
They are identical|Rate counts nucleotides per second; processivity counts additions per binding event|Processivity measures ATP per nucleotide|Rate is the total genome size
B
A rapidly catalyzing polymerase can be poorly processive if it frequently dissociates. The beta clamp principally improves retention.
B
What molecule is directly removed during epsilon-dependent editing?
A terminal misincorporated nucleotide|An entire downstream RNA primer|A DNA clamp|The entire parental strand
A
Proofreading is removal at the 3′ end of a newly made chain; Pol I's 5′ nuclease instead acts on downstream substrate.
B
Which feature is shared by both leading and lagging DNA synthesis?
Repeated priming at every fragment boundary|Synthesis away from the fork|5′ to 3′ polymerization|Absence of proofreading
C
Both synthesize DNA at a 3′ hydroxyl, both can proofread. Repeated priming is characteristic of lagging-strand execution.
B
Which protein recognizes oriC before elongation, rather than acting as the main replicative helicase?
DnaB|DnaA|DnaG|DnaN
B
DnaA is the initiation protein; DnaB unwinds, DnaG primes, and DnaN encodes the beta clamp.
B
What is nick translation?
Moving the position of a nick through coupled downstream removal and upstream synthesis|Translating DNA into protein|Helicase movement on intact duplex|Joining DNA by ATP without synthesis
A
Full-length Pol I can replace downstream RNA or DNA while extending the upstream end. The nick moves until a suitable ligase substrate is available.
B
What does the trombone model explain?
How one polymerase synthesizes DNA 3′ to 5′|How lagging-template looping coordinates fork-associated polymerases|How Tus changes into Ter|How chromosome dimers are cut by gyrase
B
Looping changes the spatial path of the template, not the chemistry or direction of synthesis.
B
Which topoisomerase can introduce negative supercoils into relaxed DNA in the canonical bacterial reaction?
E. coli DNA gyrase|E. coli Pol III|E. coli SSB|E. coli LigA
A
Gyrase uses ATP-driven type II strand passage. The other proteins do not change linking number by strand passage.
B
What is the usual order of magnitude of an E. coli Okazaki fragment?
1–2 nucleotides|10–20 nucleotides|1–2 kilonucleotides|1–2 megabases
C
Standard bacterial examples are roughly 1–2 kb, not primer-length or chromosome-length. Length is a distribution rather than a constant.
C
Two forks copy a 4.8 Mb circular chromosome at 800 bp/s each. Ignoring pauses, what is the elongation interval?
25 min|50 min|100 min|12.5 min
B
T = 4,800,000/(800 + 800) = 3,000 s = 50 min. The two rates add; using only one doubles the time.
C
A 4.8 Mb genome has mean Okazaki fragments of 1,600 nt. Estimate fragment number across two forks.
B
One nucleotide of lagging synthesis is required per parental base pair across both replichores. G/L = 4,800,000/1,600 = 3,000. The 6,000 estimate wrongly includes leading DNA.
C
A fork advances at 900 bp/s and effective primers appear every 2 s. What average fragment length is predicted by the simple model?
C
L = vΔt = 900 × 2 = 1,800 nt. The model assumes effective sequential priming and unchanged fork speed.
C
A 6 Mb chromosome has unrestricted forks moving at 1,000 and 500 bp/s. How far has the fast fork traveled at convergence?
2 Mb|3 Mb|4 Mb|6 Mb
C
T = 6,000,000/1,500 = 4,000 s. Fast distance = 4,000,000 bp. The slower fork covers the other 2 Mb.
C
Using the preceding chromosome, suppose the fast fork is arrested at 3 Mb and waits. How long from initiation to convergence?
C
The slower fork must cover 3 Mb at 500 bp/s, taking 6,000 s. Its movement occurs concurrently with the fast fork, so the two travel durations are not added.
C

A pulse produces 80% short labeled DNA. After a chase the fraction is 20%, with unchanged total label. What fraction of initially short-associated label has left the short fraction, under a simple conversion model?
C
The loss is 60 percentage points, divided by the initial 80%: 0.75. This is consistent with joining but assumes conserved label and no redistribution by degradation.
C
A mutant retains normal pulse incorporation but most label remains in short DNA after chase. Adding purified LigA alone restores long products without dNTPs. Which defect is most consistent?
Primase failure|Failure to seal suitable nicks|Loss of alpha catalysis|Failure of DNA unwinding
B
Ligase rescue without replacement synthesis indicates that suitable adjacent ends are already present. The evidence supports a sealing defect, not absent initial synthesis.
C
A derivative of Pol I fills a simple gap but cannot process a junction containing downstream RNA. Which defect is most consistent?
Loss of 5′ nuclease|Loss of all polymerase activity|Loss of ligase activity in the enzyme itself|Gain of DnaB activity
A
Gap filling establishes synthetic competence. The RNA-containing substrate additionally requires downstream processing, implicating the 5′ nuclease domain.
C
A beta-clamp mutant loads normally on DNA but fails to bind alpha. A short-template assay shows normal core catalysis. What should change most directly?
Processivity on long DNA decreases|DNA becomes RNA|Tus becomes nonpolar|All dNTP hydrolysis ceases
A
Clamp-polymerase association is necessary for retention. Normal clamp loading and intrinsic catalysis do not guarantee long-chain synthesis.
C
A loader mutant retains normal ATP binding but DNA-associated clamp signal is low. Core catalysis is normal. Which conclusion is justified?
Alpha is absent|The clamp-loading cycle is impaired, but the precise step needs further testing|DnaG synthesizes DNA|The chromosome must be completely replicated
B
The data localize the problem to productive loading or retention. They do not identify whether opening, deposition, hydrolysis or unloading is responsible.
C
An established fork is treated with a selective primase perturbation. Which early change is most plausible?
Lagging priming falls, while existing leading ends may transiently extend|Leading extension must immediately reverse|All DNA nicks are immediately sealed|The terminus disappears
A
Lagging synthesis repeatedly requires new primers. Existing leading primer ends may support a transient continuation; later fork uncoupling can affect both strands.
C
A DNA sample from a topoisomerase mutant has near-normal DNA mass, but two daughter duplex rings remain linked. Which function is most directly missing?
Origin recognition|Decatenation|Primer formation|Nucleotide selection
B
The observed lesion is an inter-duplex topological link. Topo IV is the major E. coli enzyme responsible; extra polymerization cannot remove a catenane.
C
In a simplified domain 2,100 bp are unwound with a 10.5 bp/turn repeat and no rotation. Estimate the number of type II relaxation steps, each removing two turns.
B
2,100/10.5 = 200 turns; 200/2 = 100 net events. This is a model workload, not a direct count of enzyme molecules.
C
A closed 1,050 bp plasmid has a relaxed reference Lk of 100 and actual Lk of 94. What is its superhelical density?
B
σ = (Lk−Lk0)/Lk0 = (94−100)/100 = −0.06. The negative sign indicates underlinking relative to the reference.
C
Two forks together produce 1.8 fragments/s while processing removes 1.3 fragments/s. Starting at zero, what backlog accumulates after 40 seconds if rates are constant?
A
The net rate is 0.5 fragments/s, hence 20 fragments. The other values correspond to cumulative production, removal or sums rather than backlog.
C
A 4 Mb chromosome is replicated once. How many net DNA nucleotide residues are added to all daughters combined?
2 million|4 million|8 million|16 million
C
Each of the two original template strands is 4 million nucleotides long. Net new DNA is 2G = 8 million nucleotides, excluding excised material.
C
In an orientation assay a fork passes 95% of sites without Tus. With Tus, passage is 90% in orientation X and 5% in orientation Y. Which inference is strongest?
Ter is an unconditional barrier|Tus-dependent arrest is polar in this assay|Tus is a DNA polymerase|All bacterial chromosomes require Tus
B
The strong interaction between Tus presence and orientation supports polarity. It does not establish universal necessity or catalytic identity.
C
After Tus deletion cells complete chromosome replication under standard conditions. What conclusion is warranted?
Fork convergence is impossible|Tus is not strictly required for completion under those conditions|Ter sequences must be copied as RNA|Topo IV is dispensable
B
Forks can meet without a dedicated trap. This result does not exclude conditional roles for Tus, nor does it establish that other completion enzymes are unnecessary.
C
A mutant has normal bulk DNA incorporation and increased RNA-DNA hybrid material at fragment junctions. Ligase alone gives poor rescue. What is the most useful next test?
Assay Pol I processing and test rescue with Pol I plus dNTPs and ligase|Measure only colony color|Add additional Tus|Assume all polymerases have stopped
A
The intermediate points to maturation rather than initial extension. Sequential enzyme rescue can test whether primer removal and replacement precede sealing.
C
A mutant exhibits elevated origin/terminus marker ratio. Which conclusion is valid without additional measurements?
Fork speed is definitely doubled|The ratio alone does not uniquely distinguish increased initiation from slow progression|Every cell contains exactly two forks|Pol I has been deleted
B
Both initiation frequency and replication time influence marker abundance in a population; an independent progression measurement is needed.
C
An exonuclease-defective Pol III core extends a primer almost normally but misincorporations survive more often. Which prediction best follows?
Reduced proofreading fidelity despite substantial DNA synthesis|No new phosphodiester bond can form|No clamp can load|Tus polarity reverses
A
Epsilon editing and alpha catalysis are distinct. Downstream mismatch repair can partly compensate, so the final mutation frequency is not determined solely by this assay.
C
A hypothetical inhibitor stabilizes a gyrase-DNA cleavage complex rather than merely blocking ATP turnover. What additional outcome is especially plausible?
DNA break-associated damage when forks encounter trapped complexes|Direct RNA primer synthesis|More complete decatenation|Loss of base complementarity in all DNA
A
A cleavage-complex poison retains DNA in a broken intermediate. A simple catalytic inhibitor can also stop replication but need not stabilize such breaks.
AR
Assertion: A nick may be present in a duplex with all base pairs intact. Reason: A nick is a missing covalent bond between adjacent nucleotides on one strand.
Both true; reason explains assertion|Both true; reason does not explain assertion|Assertion true, reason false|Assertion false, reason true
A
Base pairing and backbone continuity are distinct. A nick can remove a phosphodiester bond without removing a nucleotide or its base pair.
AR
Assertion: Both DNA strands are synthesized 5′ to 3′. Reason: Lagging synthesis requires repeated priming because its template orientation is opposite to fork movement for polymerization.
Both true; reason explains assertion|Both true; reason does not explain assertion|Assertion true, reason false|Assertion false, reason true
B
Both are true, but repeated priming is a solution to the pre-existing chemical constraint; it is not the reason polymerases synthesize 5′ to 3′.
AR
Assertion: Tus is obligatory for all circular bacterial chromosome termination. Reason: Tus–Ter can arrest E. coli forks in an orientation-dependent manner.
Both true; reason explains assertion|Both true; reason does not explain assertion|Assertion true, reason false|Assertion false, reason true
D
Tus–Ter polarity is established in E. coli. The universal and obligatory claim is false; other bacteria and Tus-deficient E. coli can complete replication.
AR
Assertion: Klenow can extend a correctly primed DNA template. Reason: Ordinary Klenow retains the polymerase domain of Pol I.
Both true; reason explains assertion|Both true; reason does not explain assertion|Assertion true, reason false|Assertion false, reason true
A
The C-terminal fragment retains polymerization; it lacks the N-terminal 5′ nuclease.
AR
Assertion: Topo IV can separate linked daughter duplex circles. Reason: A type II topoisomerase can pass a duplex through a transient double-strand gate.
Both true; reason explains assertion|Both true; reason does not explain assertion|Assertion true, reason false|Assertion false, reason true
A
Duplex strand passage changes inter-circle topology while allowing DNA resealing.
MS
Select the correct statements: I. DnaG makes RNA primers. II. Beta clamp is the main nuclease. III. Pol III alpha polymerizes. IV. LigA fills nucleotide gaps.
I and III|II and IV|I, II and III|All four
A
I and III correctly assign functions. Beta is a sliding tether rather than nuclease, and LigA joins adjacent termini rather than filling gaps.
MS

Select the correct statements: I. Leading and lagging roles depend on fork direction. II. Both daughter strands grow at 3′ ends. III. DnaB normally tracks the lagging template. IV. Pol III has the same 5′ nuclease as Pol I.
I, II and III|II and IV|I and IV|All four
A
The first three describe fork geometry and chemistry. IV wrongly assigns Pol I's characteristic downstream nuclease to Pol III.
MS
Which outcomes can occur even if much DNA has already been synthesized? I. Retained RNA primers. II. Unsealed DNA nicks. III. Catenated daughters. IV. Failure to have any new DNA at all.
I and II only|I, II and III|III and IV|All four
B
Maturation and topology are distinct from total synthesis. IV contradicts the premise of substantial new DNA.
MATCH
Match P DnaG, Q DnaN, R LigA, S ParC/ParE with 1 clamp, 2 priming, 3 decatenation, 4 sealing.
P2 Q1 R4 S3|P1 Q2 R3 S4|P4 Q3 R1 S2|P3 Q4 R2 S1
A
DnaG creates RNA primers, DnaN is the beta clamp, LigA seals nicks and ParC/ParE make Topo IV.
MATCH
Match P Pol I, Q Pol III ε, R gyrase, S Tus with 1 negative supercoiling, 2 downstream primer processing, 3 polar barrier, 4 terminal proofreading.
P2 Q4 R1 S3|P4 Q2 R3 S1|P1 Q3 R2 S4|P3 Q1 R4 S2
A
Pol I processes downstream nucleic acid, epsilon edits a 3′ terminus, gyrase controls supercoiling and Tus binds Ter.
C
A chromosome has 3,000 fragments with mean 12-nt primers. If each primer is fully replaced and no extra DNA is removed, how many dNTPs are incorporated specifically in replacement?
C
Each RNA position requires a DNA residue, 3,000 × 12 = 36,000. Actual processing can replace additional downstream DNA, which is excluded by the premise.
C
Two complete chromosome copies are covalently joined into one doubled-length circle. Which operation directly resolves this structure in E. coli?
Decatenation of two independent circles alone|XerCD-mediated site-specific dimer resolution|Adding a beta clamp|Repeated primer formation
B
The product is a covalent dimer, not two linked rings. Site-specific recombination can resolve it; Topo IV strand passage alone does not split a covalent dimer.
C
In a trap experiment, a clamp-free core adds 40 nt/s for 0.25 s per association; a clamp-bound core adds 40 nt/s for 25 s. What changes under this model?
Rate increases 100-fold|Processivity increases from 10 to 1,000 nt while rate stays constant|Rate falls 100-fold|Both complexes have the same processivity
B
Multiplying the bound lifetime by the instantaneous rate gives the expected additions per binding. The clamp increases retention, not the stipulated catalytic speed.
C
A sample of 1,000 correctly formed DNA-only nicks is sealed through fully regenerated LigA cycles. Ignoring initially adenylated enzyme, how many NAD+ molecules are consumed?
B
One NAD+ supplies the adenylation intermediate for each complete successful ligation cycle. The number would differ if initially activated enzyme were counted separately.
C
A new strand has an upstream 3′-OH and adjacent downstream 5′-OH rather than 5′ phosphate. Adding LigA does not seal it. Which inference is appropriate?

LigA is necessarily inactive|The end chemistry is unsuitable; phosphorylation must precede ordinary nick ligation|The duplex cannot contain complementary bases|Pol III must add a nucleotide at the 5′ end
B
LigA needs an appropriate 5′ phosphate to form DNA-adenylate. A failed reaction using an unsuitable substrate does not establish enzyme inactivity.
